questions.stem: Which behaviour best shows the skill of building on another student's opinion?
options: Repeating your own earlier opinion louder so the group returns to it
Restating the previous point in your own words, then adding an example
Waiting for the speaker to finish, then raising a point about another text
Agreeing briefly so the group can move on to the next question
questions.explanation: Building on a contribution means acknowledging what was said, showing you understood it, and extending it with new evidence or reasoning. Introducing a completely new point about a different text is polite turn-taking but not building, because nothing connects the new contribution to the previous one. The cue is the word 'build': your contribution must stand on the previous one, usually signalled by phrases like 'adding to that' or 'following on from'.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say that language features 'position' an audience?
options: They match the reading level of the text to the age group of the intended audience
They shape how readers or viewers are invited to feel about and judge what is presented
They arrange information in the order the audience will find easiest to remember
They tell the audience directly what opinion the writer holds about the subject
questions.explanation: Positioning refers to the way word choice, tone, imagery and structure guide an audience towards a particular attitude or judgement, often without the audience noticing. The idea that the writer tells the audience directly what they think is tempting, but positioning usually works through implication and connotation rather than open statement. If the effect is stated outright it is simply the writer's opinion; positioning is how the text nudges you to share it.

questions.stem: A newspaper opinion piece describes a proposed skate park as 'a magnet for trouble'. What is the main effect of this metaphor on readers?
options: It signals that the writer is presenting a balanced view of both sides of the proposal
It defines the term 'skate park' more precisely for readers unfamiliar with the facility
It suggests the park will unavoidably attract antisocial behaviour, without offering evidence
It provides a statistic about crime rates near skate parks in comparable suburbs
questions.explanation: A metaphor with negative connotations does persuasive work: 'magnet' implies an automatic, irresistible pull, so trouble is presented as inevitable rather than argued for. Reading it as balanced is wrong because the phrase carries only one attitude and offers no counterview. When a vivid image replaces evidence, the writer is positioning rather than proving.

questions.stem: A student says: 'I don't agree she's unreliable — on page 42 she admits she was asleep.' Which skill is that?
options: Challenging an opinion by grounding the disagreement in textual evidence
Clarifying an unclear point by asking the speaker to explain further
Summarising the discussion so far before moving to a new question
Conceding a point in order to keep the discussion moving forward
questions.explanation: She states disagreement and then supports it with a specific reference from the text, which is the hallmark of evidence-based challenge in discussion. Clarifying is wrong because she asks no question and seeks no further explanation from the other speaker. Look for a question mark for clarifying; look for a page reference or quotation for evidence-based challenge.

questions.stem: An advertisement for a charity uses the second person: 'You can end her hunger today.' What effect does this pronoun choice have on the audience?
options: It signals that the advertisement is aimed only at people who already donate
It makes each viewer feel personally responsible for and capable of the outcome
It establishes the charity's expertise by emphasising its long record of aid work
It creates distance so the viewer can judge the appeal objectively before donating
questions.explanation: Direct address with 'you' singles out the individual viewer, converting a general problem into a personal choice and making inaction feel like a decision. The 'creates distance' option reverses the effect: second person closes distance rather than opening it. Whenever you see 'you' in persuasive text, ask what the viewer is being made responsible for.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest statement of a persuasive text's purpose and audience?
options: To explain, for council engineers, how the pool's filtration works
To persuade local residents to oppose the closure of the pool
To describe the pool and list its opening hours for swimmers
To entertain readers with a humorous story set at the pool
questions.explanation: Purpose is what the text is trying to do to or for readers, and audience is who it is aimed at; a persuasive text sets out to change the reader's position, so 'persuade local residents to oppose the closure' names both a persuasive purpose and a specific audience. The most tempting alternative is the one about describing the pool and listing opening hours, because it also names an audience, but its purpose is informing, not persuading, so it does not fit a persuasive text. The cue is the verb at the start: persuade, entertain, inform and explain each signal a different purpose.

questions.stem: A council media release states: 'Regrettably, a small number of residents have been inconvenienced by the necessary upgrade works.' Analysing how this language positions readers, which statement is accurate?
options: The noun 'residents' is technical jargon that positions readers to feel excluded from the council's decision
The quantifier 'a small number' and the adjective 'necessary' minimise the disruption and frame the works as unavoidable
The passive construction 'have been inconvenienced' names the council directly as the party responsible for the disruption
The adverb 'regrettably' is an emotive appeal that positions readers to see the upgrade works as a mistake
questions.explanation: Positioning works through small word choices: 'a small number' shrinks the scale of the complaint and 'necessary' presents the works as something no one could reasonably object to, so readers are nudged towards accepting the council's view. The tempting distractor is the claim about the passive construction, but a passive like 'have been inconvenienced' actually leaves the agent unnamed, doing the opposite of naming the council. When you meet a passive verb, ask who has been left out of the sentence — that omission is usually the point.

questions.stem: In an oral presentation, which of the following is a feature of voice rather than a multimodal element?
options: A printed handout summarising the key statistics
Pitch variation used to signal a shift to a new point
A slide showing a labelled diagram of the process
A short video clip played to introduce the topic
questions.explanation: Features of voice are the vocal choices a speaker makes while speaking — volume, pace, pitch, tone, emphasis and pause — so varying pitch to mark a new point is a voice feature. The slide with a labelled diagram is tempting because it is part of the same presentation, but it is a visual (multimodal) element, not something produced by the voice. The cue is to ask whether the audience hears it in how the words are said, or sees or reads it alongside the words.

questions.stem: A student is giving a formal speech to the school council. Which opening matches that formality?
options: Look, you all know the canteen's rubbish, so let's just fix it.
Good afternoon. I am here to propose three changes to the menu.
Hey everyone, so basically the canteen is pretty average right now.
Righto, listen up, because the canteen food situation is a joke.
questions.explanation: Formality is adjusted for audience and context: a school council is an official decision-making body, so the speech should use standard English, full sentences and a courteous greeting before stating the proposal. The 'Hey everyone, so basically' opening is the most tempting because it sounds friendly and confident, but colloquialisms such as 'basically' and 'pretty average' suit a casual peer audience, not a formal proposal. Check who holds the authority in the situation: the more official the audience, the more formal the register.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say a spoken text is 'structured'?
options: It uses formal vocabulary and avoids all contractions throughout
It is supported at every stage by slides and digital images
It is organised with a clear opening, sequenced points and a closing
It is delivered word for word from a fully written script
questions.explanation: Structure refers to the organisation of ideas — an introduction that orients the audience, body points in a deliberate order with signposting, and a conclusion that resolves the talk. Reading word for word from a script is the most tempting answer because scripted talks often are well organised, but a script controls wording, not organisation, and an unscripted talk can still be tightly structured. Ask whether the feature concerns the ordering of ideas or the manner of delivery.

questions.stem: A student pauses for two seconds after asking her audience, 'So how many of those bottles do you think we throw away each week?' What is the most likely purpose of this pause?
options: To reduce the overall formality of the presentation for a peer audience
To give the audience a moment to think before she reveals the figure
To signal to the audience that her presentation has finished
To indicate that she has lost her place and needs to check her notes
questions.explanation: A deliberate pause after a rhetorical question creates anticipation and invites the listeners to form their own answer, which makes the statistic that follows land harder. The 'lost her place' option is tempting because unplanned pauses do happen, but a pause placed straight after a question is a recognised persuasive technique, not a stumble. The cue is placement: a pause at a meaningful boundary is a choice, while one mid-clause usually is not.

questions.stem: A student's slides for a five-minute talk each contain about 150 words of text, which he reads aloud. Which criticism of this multimodal choice is accurate?
options: Reading aloud from slides is acceptable only if the speaker faces the screen
The slides compete with his speech, so the audience reads instead of listening
The slides are too formal for a classroom audience and should be removed
Using slides at all means the text is no longer a structured spoken text
questions.explanation: Digital elements should support and extend the spoken text, so dense slides duplicated word for word split the audience's attention between reading and listening and weaken both. Saying the slides are 'too formal' is tempting because the problem does feel like a mismatch, but the issue is the amount of text and its duplication of speech, not the register. Effective slides carry an image, a keyword or a figure that the speaker then explains.

questions.stem: Two students give the same talk on local transport: one to a Year 7 assembly, one to a council transport committee. Which adjustment is the most appropriate for the council version?
options: Use precise technical terms and cite the source of each statistic
Speak more slowly throughout and repeat every key point twice
Add more humour and personal anecdotes to hold the committee's attention
Remove all visual support so the committee focuses on the argument
questions.explanation: Adapting to audience means matching vocabulary, evidence and register to what listeners know and expect; a council committee is an expert, decision-making audience that expects accurate terminology and sourced data. Adding humour and anecdotes is tempting because engagement matters everywhere, but it is the Year 7 assembly that most needs that lightening, while the committee needs credibility. Ask what the audience already knows and what they need in order to act.

questions.stem: A student ends a persuasive speech by dropping her volume slightly and slowing her pace on the final sentence. What is the most likely effect of these vocal choices?
options: It signals to the audience that she is running out of prepared material
It marks the closing statement as significant and draws listeners in
It shows uncertainty, so the audience discounts the final claim
It raises the formality of the whole speech retrospectively
questions.explanation: Controlled contrast in volume and pace is an emphasis technique: slowing and softening at the end forces closer attention and gives the closing idea weight. The 'shows uncertainty' option is tempting because quiet speech can read as nervousness, but here the change is deliberate, localised to the final sentence and paired with slower pace, which is the pattern of a planned close. Look for whether the vocal change is sustained and unintended or brief and purposeful.

questions.stem: Which sentence from a speech to a formal community forum best shows a shift in formality that still suits the audience?
options: 'The data's a mess, but whatever, you get what I'm saying.'
'The data is clear, hey, and no one's really arguing about that.'
'The data is clear. Put simply: we are running out of time.'
'The data, as any reasonable person would concede, is frankly beyond dispute.'
questions.explanation: Skilled speakers can drop briefly into plainer, more direct language for emphasis while keeping the overall register formal, and 'Put simply: we are running out of time' does exactly that without slang or dismissiveness. The heavily qualified 'as any reasonable person would concede' option is tempting because it sounds the most formal, but piling on formal phrasing is not a shift in formality and its wording also pressures the audience rather than informing them. Look for a controlled move toward plainness, not for maximum formality or for slang.

questions.stem: In English, what does 'representation' mean when analysing a text?
options: How a text constructs a version of people or events through choices
How a reader summarises the main events accurately in their own words
How a text is adapted into another form, such as a film or novel
How an author's real experiences are recorded truthfully in fiction
questions.explanation: A representation is a constructed version of reality: a writer or maker selects details, language and images, so what reaches the audience is shaped rather than neutral. The option about summarising confuses representation with comprehension — summarising is what a reader does, while representation is what the text does. The cue is the word 'constructs': ask what has been selected, emphasised or left out.

questions.stem: When analysts talk about the 'context' that a representation reflects, they mean:
options: The genre conventions a text must follow to be classified correctly by librarians
The intended length and format a publisher requires before a text is printed
The social, historical and cultural circumstances in which a text was produced and read
The paragraphs immediately before and after a quotation used in an essay
questions.explanation: Context refers to the values, beliefs, events and conditions surrounding a text's production and reception, which shape how people and places are portrayed. The option about surrounding paragraphs describes 'context' in its everyday reading sense — useful for working out word meaning, but not what contextual analysis means. If the question is about time, place and values, you are dealing with context in the curriculum sense.

questions.stem: A 1950s Australian magazine article describes a young woman's ambition as 'finding a good husband and a tidy home'. What does this representation most clearly reflect?
options: The fact that no Australian women worked outside the home during the 1950s
The magazine's need to shorten the article to fit the space available on the page
The gender expectations widely held in Australian society at the time of writing
The personal dislike the individual writer felt towards women seeking careers
questions.explanation: Representations carry the assumptions of their era, and this portrayal treats domestic life as a woman's natural goal — a value widely circulating in 1950s Australia. The option about the writer's personal dislike is tempting because a person wrote the words, but analysis of context looks past individual feeling to the shared values the text takes for granted. Ask whether the text assumes readers will agree; if so, you are seeing context, not just opinion.

questions.stem: Two travel texts describe the same outback town. One calls it 'empty and desolate'; the other calls it 'Country that has sustained families for generations'. The difference in these representations is best explained by:
options: The different cultural perspectives and values the two writers bring to the place
One writer being factually accurate while the other has made a clear error
The fact that the writers visited the town in two different seasons of the year
One text being fiction and the other text being a piece of non-fiction writing
questions.explanation: The same place can be represented very differently depending on the writer's relationship to it, and word choice reveals those underlying values — 'empty' assumes absence, 'sustained' assumes long connection. The accuracy option is tempting because the descriptions clash, but neither is a factual error; they are different framings of the same location. When two texts conflict in tone rather than in facts, look for differing perspectives.

questions.stem: A news photograph of a protest is cropped so that only a small group of shouting people is visible, though the crowd stretched for two blocks. What is the effect of this choice on the representation?
options: It proves the photographer personally disagreed with everything the protesters said
It makes the image factually false, since photographs cannot show a viewpoint
It has no effect on meaning, because the caption will explain the true situation
It represents the protest as small and aggressive rather than large and organised
questions.explanation: Framing and cropping are selection choices: what is left out of an image shapes the version of the event the audience receives, here shrinking a large protest to a handful of angry figures. The claim that the photographer personally disagreed goes further than the evidence allows — a selection choice shows an effect, not a proven private motive. Analyse what the choice does to the audience's impression before speculating about intent.

questions.stem: Which question best analyses how a text's representation of a group reflects its context?
options: Which genre does the text belong to, and when was that genre invented?
Whose perspectives are given voice here, and whose are absent?
How many paragraphs describe each of the characters?
Does the text use correct spelling, punctuation and grammar?
questions.explanation: Asking who speaks and who is silenced exposes the assumptions and power relations of the context in which a text was made, which is the heart of this kind of analysis. Counting paragraphs looks analytical but measures quantity, not the values a text carries; a group could be described at length and still be represented narrowly. The cue is that contextual analysis asks about voice, values and absence.

questions.stem: A 2024 film sets a well-known nineteenth-century novel in the present day and gives the heroine a career of her own. This change to the representation most directly reflects:
options: The original author's private intentions, finally made clear for modern viewers
A rule that all film adaptations must update their source material's settings
The values of the contemporary context in which the adaptation was produced
A mistake by the filmmakers, who have misread the original novel's plot events
questions.explanation: Adaptations are made in a new context, so they reshape characters and events in ways that make sense to present-day audiences and reflect present-day values. The option about the author's private intentions is tempting because adaptations often claim fidelity, but a change made two centuries later reflects the adapters' context, not recovered authorial intent. Ask which era's values the change serves — that identifies whose context is being reflected.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The novel represents the mining town as doomed, using decay imagery, which reflects anxieties about industrial decline in the 1980s.' Why is this a stronger analysis than saying 'The town in the novel is sad and run-down'?
options: It states a personal opinion about the town, which analysis always requires
It avoids naming the setting, which keeps the analysis general and therefore safer
It links a specific textual choice to the values and concerns of a particular context
It uses a longer sentence, which examiners consistently reward with higher marks
questions.explanation: Analysis of representation requires three moves: name the choice, name the effect, and connect it to context — this response does all three, while the weaker version only describes content. The claim about longer sentences is tempting because the strong answer is longer, but length alone adds nothing; a long sentence that only retells events is still description. Check that a contextual link is present, not just extra words.

questions.stem: In text analysis, what are 'evaluative words'?
options: Words that carry a judgement of worth, such as 'reckless', 'admirable' or 'shameful'
Words that state measurable facts, such as 'twelve', 'Tuesday' or 'kilometre'
Words that join clauses together, such as 'however', 'because' or 'although'
Words that name an action or state, such as 'ran', 'believes' or 'became'
questions.explanation: Evaluative words encode the writer's judgement of how good, bad, worthy or unworthy something is, so they are one of the most direct ways a text signals attitudes. The option about words joining clauses describes connectives, which structure an argument but do not themselves carry judgement. The cue is to ask whether the word could be replaced by a neutral synonym without losing an opinion — if it could, the original was evaluative.

questions.stem: A text uses high modality when it contains words like:
options: 'quickly', 'loudly' and 'suddenly'
'must', 'certainly' and 'never'
'might', 'possibly' and 'sometimes'
'she', 'they' and 'we'
questions.explanation: Modality is the degree of certainty or obligation a writer commits to, and words like 'must', 'certainly' and 'never' sit at the high end, presenting a belief as beyond question. The set 'might', 'possibly' and 'sometimes' is the opposite — low modality, which hedges a claim. Remember that high modality closes off doubt, so it makes an attitude sound like settled fact.

questions.stem: A newspaper report describes striking workers as 'a mob of agitators' while the same event is reported elsewhere as 'a gathering of concerned staff'. What does this difference in word choice most clearly show?
options: Only the second report contains language features; the first is neutral reporting
The reports were written for readers in different countries rather than for different purposes
The two reports use different connotations to represent opposing attitudes to the strike
The first report is factually inaccurate and the second is factually accurate
questions.explanation: Both phrases denote the same group of people, but 'mob of agitators' carries associations of disorder while 'concerned staff' carries associations of reasonableness, so connotation is carrying the attitude. Claiming the first report is factually inaccurate confuses attitude with truth — a text can describe real events while still framing them judgementally. Ask what each word suggests about the people, not whether the event happened.

questions.stem: An editorial argues: 'We all know that hard work deserves reward.' Which analysis of the language features here is accurate?
options: The inclusive pronoun distances readers from the writer's belief so they can judge it freely
The phrase 'hard work' is emotive language that makes the claim impossible to dispute
The sentence is a factual statement, so it contains no attitudinal language features
The inclusive pronoun and high-modality phrase present a contested belief as shared common sense
questions.explanation: 'We all' assumes the reader already agrees, and 'know' asserts certainty, so together they dress an opinion up as something everybody accepts. The option saying the pronoun distances readers reverses the actual effect of inclusive language, which draws readers inside the writer's position. When you see 'we' plus a certainty verb, check whether an arguable belief is being smuggled in as an obvious truth.

questions.stem: A media release states: 'The relocation of families occurred following the redevelopment decision.' Evaluating this use of nominalisation, which statement is accurate?
options: Turning actions into nouns is simply a grammatical error that adds no attitudinal effect
Turning actions into nouns increases the certainty of the claim by raising its modality
Turning actions into nouns removes the people responsible, making a contested decision seem impersonal
Turning actions into nouns makes the writing more emotive by emphasising the families' distress
questions.explanation: Nominalisation packs a process ('someone relocated the families', 'someone decided') into a noun, and in doing so it can delete the agent, so responsibility disappears from the sentence. The option about emphasising distress is tempting because families are mentioned, but the abstract noun 'relocation' actually drains the human experience out of the event. The cue is to ask 'who did this?' — if the sentence cannot say, nominalisation is masking an agent.

questions.stem: What is meant by the 'connotation' of a word?
options: The repetition of the same consonant sound at the start of words
The certainty or obligation a word signals, such as 'must' or 'might'
The associations and feelings it carries beyond its literal meaning
The literal dictionary meaning, stripped of any associations
questions.explanation: Connotation refers to the attitudes, judgements and feelings attached to a word by its use in a culture, which is why 'thrifty' and 'stingy' can describe the same behaviour while carrying opposite evaluations. The option about the literal dictionary meaning is the most tempting, but that describes denotation, the plain reference of a word before associations are added. A useful cue: denotation answers 'what does it point to?', connotation answers 'how does it make the reader feel about it?'

questions.stem: In expository writing, what is the main job of a topic sentence?
options: It signals the writer's opinion, so readers can tell fact from opinion
It states the central idea the paragraph will develop, guiding the reader
It provides the most detailed evidence, so readers can check the research
It summarises the whole text, so readers can skip the other paragraphs
questions.explanation: A topic sentence announces the controlling idea of a paragraph; the sentences that follow expand, illustrate or qualify it, which is what allows a reader to track how ideas are organised across a text. The option about summarising the whole text confuses a topic sentence with a thesis statement, which appears once, usually in the introduction, and governs every paragraph rather than one. The cue: a topic sentence controls one paragraph, a thesis controls the whole text.

questions.stem: What do writers use cohesive devices such as 'however', 'as a result' and 'in the same way' to do?
options: Mark the point where a new section of the text begins
Signal the logical relationship between one idea and the next
Raise the formality of the writing to suit an academic audience
Replace evidence that the writer has not been able to locate
questions.explanation: Connectives of this kind name the relationship between ideas — contrast, cause and effect, comparison — so readers can follow the shape of the reasoning. The formality option is tempting because these words do sound formal, but plenty of informal writing uses 'however' and plenty of formal writing avoids it; formality is a by-product, not the function. Ask what relationship the word names, not how it sounds.

questions.stem: A feature article opens with a two-sentence account of one family losing their home in a flood, before moving to statistics and policy. What is the most likely effect of placing the anecdote first?
options: It signals that the article is fiction, so readers approach the statistics with scepticism
It establishes the writer's expertise, so readers accept the policy claims without evidence
It engages readers emotionally, so the later statistics are read as evidence of a human problem
It proves the argument at the outset, so the statistics that follow are not strictly needed
questions.explanation: Placement matters: an opening anecdote frames everything after it, giving the abstract data a human reference point and making the reader more receptive to the argument. The option claiming the anecdote proves the argument is wrong because a single case is illustrative, not proof — the statistics do the work of showing scale. When evaluating structure, ask what the first element makes the reader feel or expect about what follows.

questions.stem: A student's paragraph moves from a claim about isolation in a novel, to a quotation, to an explanation of the quotation, to a link back to the claim. What does this organisation most clearly achieve?
options: It varies the subject matter within the paragraph, so the writing avoids sounding repetitive
It delays the main point until the end, so the reader is kept in suspense
It separates analysis from evidence, so the reader can assess each independently
It keeps every sentence working on one idea, so the evidence is visibly tied to the claim
questions.explanation: This is a unified paragraph: the claim controls it, the quotation supports it, the explanation interprets it and the link closes the loop, so the reader can see exactly why the evidence counts. The 'delays the main point' option misreads the structure — the claim comes first, not last. The cue is where the controlling idea sits: front-loaded claim means unity, not suspense.

questions.stem: A researcher's report is arranged under the headings Background, Method, Findings, Recommendations. What kind of organisational structure is this, and what does it do for the reader?
options: A comparative structure that sets two positions against each other for the reader to judge
A cyclical structure that returns to its opening idea to give the report a sense of closure
A functional structure that lets readers locate the section they need without reading the whole report
A chronological structure that recounts events in the order the researcher experienced them
questions.explanation: Headings that name the function of each section — what it is for, rather than when it happened — let a reader enter the document at the point that serves their purpose, which is why reports are built this way. Chronological is the tempting choice because research does happen in roughly that order, but the headings label roles in the report, not a sequence of events, and readers are expected to skip about. Ask whether the sections name times or jobs.

questions.stem: An essay's final paragraph introduces a completely new piece of evidence that has not been mentioned earlier. Evaluating this structural choice, which statement is accurate?
options: It strengthens the conclusion, because ending on fresh material leaves the reader with the newest information
It has no effect on meaning, because conclusions only restate what the body paragraphs have argued
It converts the conclusion into a topic sentence, because new evidence always begins a new argument
It undermines the conclusion's function, because the evidence arrives with no space left to develop or connect it
questions.explanation: A conclusion's role is to consolidate — to draw the developed lines of argument together — so unexplained new evidence at that point leaves the reader with a loose end rather than a resolution. The option claiming conclusions 'only restate' is false: strong conclusions synthesise and draw out implications rather than simply repeating. Test any last paragraph by asking whether it closes ideas already built or opens ones it cannot support.

questions.stem: In a piece of extended writing, what does starting a new paragraph most reliably signal to the reader?
options: That the writer is moving to a new idea, or a new stage of the same idea
That the writer has reached roughly the expected length for one paragraph
That the writer has finished the argument and is moving to the conclusion
That the writer is about to introduce a quotation from another source
questions.explanation: Paragraphing organises meaning: a break tells the reader that one unit of thought is complete and another step is beginning, which is why paragraph boundaries help readers follow an argument. The most tempting wrong answer is the one about reaching the expected length — length is a rough side effect of developing an idea fully, not the reason a break happens, and writers vary paragraph length deliberately for emphasis. Ask what changes at the break: if the idea or stage shifts, the break is doing its job.

questions.stem: A persuasive feature article presents four case studies and a set of statistics first, and only states its central claim — that the state should fund free public transport for students — in the final two paragraphs. Evaluating this organisational choice, which statement is accurate?
options: Delaying the claim removes the writer's position from the text, making the article objective rather than persuasive in effect
Delaying the claim is a structural error, because a persuasive text must always announce its contention in the opening paragraph
Delaying the claim lets readers accept the evidence on its own terms first, so they are more likely to accept the conclusion it leads to
Delaying the claim means the article has no thesis, so it functions as a report rather than as a piece of persuasive writing
questions.explanation: Where a writer places the main claim changes how readers process everything else: build the evidence first and readers form impressions before they know what those impressions are being used to support, which makes resistance less likely. The claim that the article has no thesis is tempting but false — the thesis is present, just positioned late. Note also that selecting and ordering evidence towards a conclusion is itself persuasive, so a delayed claim does not make a text objective; there is no rule that the contention must come first.

questions.stem: A student reading a report on coastal erosion stops and thinks, 'This is like the story I read about the town losing its beach — the same causes are described.' Which comprehension strategy is she using?
options: Visualising
Monitoring
Connecting
Predicting
questions.explanation: Connecting means linking a text to another text, to personal experience or to wider knowledge of the world, which is exactly what comparing the report to a previously read story does. Predicting is tempting, but a prediction is a forecast about what will come next in the text, and she makes no forecast. Look for the word 'like' or 'reminds me of' as the signal of connecting.

questions.stem: A student reads: 'Mira set the letter down, walked to the window, and did not turn around when her brother said her name.' She decides Mira is upset by the letter's contents. What has the student done?
options: Made an inference from the character's actions, since the text never states her feelings
Visualised the scene, since she has built a mental image of Mira at the window
Summarised the passage, since she has captured the events in a single sentence
Predicted the outcome, since she has worked out what happens after the passage ends
questions.explanation: The text reports only actions; the emotional state is a conclusion the reader draws from those clues, which is inference. Visualising is tempting because the passage is highly visual, but visualising means constructing the picture itself, not deducing an unstated feeling from it. If your answer names something the text never says, you have inferred.

questions.stem: A student compares two articles on youth crime and writes: 'Both texts agree the rate has risen, but Article A blames a lack of youth services while Article B blames weak sentencing.' Why is this a stronger comparison than writing 'Both articles are about youth crime, but they say different things'?
options: It identifies a shared point and names the specific difference in each writer's explanation
It uses a longer sentence, which shows a more sophisticated writing style to the marker
It quotes directly from both articles, which is always required in a comparison
It evaluates which of the two articles is more persuasive for a general audience
questions.explanation: Comparing and contrasting ideas requires naming precisely where texts converge and where they diverge, and this response does both by identifying the agreed fact and the two competing causes. The option about evaluating persuasiveness is tempting, but the given response makes no judgement about which article is better, so that cannot be the reason it is stronger. Also note that no direct quotation appears in the response at all.

questions.stem: Halfway through a dense report, a student realises she cannot recall anything from the last page. She goes back, reads the subheadings, jots one line per section, then continues. Which combination of strategies best describes what she has done?
options: Monitoring, then summarising to repair her understanding
Predicting, then connecting to her prior knowledge
Questioning, then inferring the writer's unstated position
Visualising, then evaluating the writer's evidence
questions.explanation: Noticing that comprehension has failed is monitoring, and condensing each section into a line to rebuild meaning is summarising used as a repair strategy. The option naming questioning and inferring is tempting because rereading often raises questions, but she draws no unstated conclusion about the writer's position — she is recovering the stated content. The giveaway for monitoring is the moment of self-noticing, and for summarising the act of condensing.

questions.stem: When a reader uses the comprehension strategy of summarising, what are they doing?
options: Working out information the writer has implied but not stated directly
Restating the main ideas of a section in a condensed form, in their own words
Forming a picture in their mind of the setting and events being described
Guessing what the writer will say next based on clues already given
questions.explanation: Summarising means reducing a text to its key ideas, leaving out examples and detail, usually in the reader's own words. The option about working out unstated information describes inferring, which is tempting because both involve going beyond the exact words — but inferring adds meaning the writer left out, while summarising subtracts detail the writer put in. The cue is direction: summarising shrinks what is on the page, inferring reads between the lines.

questions.stem: A student reads the first two paragraphs of a news feature about a drought and thinks, 'The writer keeps mentioning the empty dam, so the article will probably argue for water restrictions.' Which comprehension strategy is she using?
options: Visualising
Predicting
Monitoring
Summarising
questions.explanation: Predicting means using clues already in the text, plus prior knowledge, to anticipate what will come next. Monitoring is tempting because she is clearly paying close attention, but monitoring means checking whether your own understanding is holding up and repairing it when it breaks down — she reports no breakdown. The cue for predicting is that the thought points forward to text not yet read.

questions.stem: Two opinion pieces both oppose lowering the voting age. A student wants to compare and contrast them properly rather than just describe them. Which note best does this?
options: The first text is well written and persuasive, while the second text is boring and repetitive
The first text was published in March and the second in June, and both are about 800 words long
Both reject the change, but one bases this on maturity and the other on the risk of low turnout
Both texts are about the voting age and both are written by adult commentators for newspapers
questions.explanation: Comparing and contrasting ideas and opinions means identifying where the positions agree and then pinpointing how the reasoning behind them differs. The note about both being newspaper pieces by adult commentators is tempting because it does state a similarity, but it compares publication features rather than ideas, so no contrast of opinion emerges. The cue is whether your sentence names the reasons or evidence each writer uses, not just the topic or the packaging.

questions.stem: While reading a science article, a student writes in the margin: 'Why does the writer only quote farmers and never quote hydrologists?' Which statement best describes what this questioning is doing for her comprehension?
options: It is confirming that she has visualised the setting of the article accurately in her mind
It is a sign she has misunderstood the article, since good readers resolve questions rather than record them
It is summarising the article's main claim in the form of a question for later revision
It is prompting her to notice whose views the text includes and excludes, which helps her weigh its argument
questions.explanation: Questioning during reading includes interrogating the text's choices — who is quoted, what is left out — and that directly supports evaluating how convincing an argument is. The claim that recording questions signals misunderstanding is tempting because students often think questions mean confusion, but skilled readers deliberately generate questions about sources and gaps even when they follow the text perfectly. The cue is that her question is about the writer's decisions, not about a word or sentence she could not follow.

questions.stem: In a persuasive text, what is the job of the thesis statement?
options: It gives background facts about the topic so readers understand the issue
It states the writer's overall point of view so the rest of the text can support it
It lists every source the writer consulted so readers can check the research
It summarises the opposing side's case so readers can judge it fairly
questions.explanation: A thesis statement declares the position the whole text will advance, giving the argument a clear spine that each paragraph then illustrates or expands. 'It summarises the opposing side's case' describes a concession or rebuttal section, which responds to other views rather than stating your own. Background facts belong in an introduction's context sentences, and source lists belong in a reference list. The cue is that a thesis can be argued with — a fact or a summary of someone else's view cannot.

questions.stem: In an argumentative essay, what is a writer doing when they include a rebuttal?
options: Acknowledging an opposing argument and then explaining why it does not hold
Restating their own main claim in stronger words at the end of the essay
Providing statistics from a study that directly support their own position
Defining the key terms of the debate before the argument properly begins
questions.explanation: A rebuttal names a view held by the other side and then dismantles it, which strengthens the writer's own case by showing it survives challenge. 'Restating their own main claim in stronger words' describes a reinforcing conclusion, not a rebuttal, because nothing opposing has been raised. Supporting statistics are evidence and definitions are clarification; neither engages with an opposing view. The cue is that a rebuttal always contains two moves: concede, then counter.

questions.stem: A student is writing an opinion piece for the school newsletter, read mainly by parents, arguing that homework should be reduced. Which supporting move best suits that audience?
options: Linking reduced homework to family time and evening wellbeing at home
Describing how much students dislike homework compared with weekends
Listing the subjects in which the writer personally receives the most work
Explaining that teachers would have fewer assignments left to correct
questions.explanation: Advancing an idea for a specific audience means choosing support that connects to what that audience values, and parents reading a newsletter are directly invested in home life and their children's wellbeing. 'Describing how much students dislike homework' is tempting because it is true of the writer's peers, but dislike alone gives parents no reason to change their view — it reads as complaint rather than argument. The personal subject list is anecdote about one student, and teacher marking loads are not a parent concern. Ask: what does this reader already care about?

questions.stem: A student is building a digital text arguing for more bike lanes and wants to use hyperlinks well. Which use of hyperlinks best serves both the argument and the reader?
options: Linking the heading of each section to the top of the same web page
Linking the writer's main claim to a video that repeats the same claim
Linking a cited council traffic figure to the report the figure comes from
Linking every second sentence to a related news story on cycling generally
questions.explanation: In digital texts, hyperlinks work best when they let a reader verify or extend a specific piece of evidence without interrupting the flow of the argument. Linking every second sentence is the tempting 'more is better' option, but dense linking fragments the reading and buries the claim under loosely related material. Links back to the top of the same page add no information, and a video that only repeats the claim expands nothing. Test each link by asking what new work it does for the reader.

questions.stem: A Year 9 student must present a five-minute argument to Year 6 students about joining a sports club. Which adjustment shows deliberate consideration of that audience?
options: Using short sentences, concrete examples and a clear repeated main message
Using specialist terms from sports science with definitions read out afterwards
Speaking faster to fit more supporting evidence into the five minutes available
Removing all humour so the presentation keeps a serious and formal register
questions.explanation: Adjusting for a younger audience means matching sentence length, vocabulary and the amount of abstraction to what they can follow, while repeating the central message so it sticks. 'Specialist terms with definitions read out afterwards' seems considerate, but front-loading unfamiliar jargon still loses the listener before the definition arrives. Speaking faster reduces comprehension rather than improving it, and humour is often an asset with younger audiences, not something to strip out. Audience adjustment is about accessibility, not just formality.

questions.stem: A student's persuasive presentation includes an infographic showing that library visits fell 40% over five years. She leaves it on screen for eight seconds without referring to it. Evaluating this choice, which statement is accurate?
options: The visual is effective, because statistics presented visually always speak for themselves without commentary
The visual is inappropriate, because numerical data should never appear in a spoken presentation
The visual is misleading, because percentages cannot be shown accurately in infographic form
The visual is underused, because unexplained data leaves the audience to guess its relevance to her claim
questions.explanation: In an effective multimodal text the modes work together: the speech has to tell the audience what the image proves and how it advances the argument, or the link between evidence and claim is never made. 'Statistics presented visually always speak for themselves' is the tempting option because good graphics are clear, but clarity about what the number is does not establish why it matters here. Data is entirely appropriate in spoken presentations, and percentages are routinely represented accurately in graphics. The test is whether the words and the visual are doing different, complementary work.

questions.stem: In a text presenting a point of view, what is the writer's 'point of view'?
options: The person the text is written in, such as first person or third person
The range of opinions already held by the audience being addressed
The position the writer takes on an issue, which the text works to support
The topic the text deals with, introduced neutrally for readers to decide
questions.explanation: A point of view in a persuasive or argumentative text is a stance — an arguable position on an issue — and everything that follows should advance, illustrate or expand it. The most tempting wrong choice is the one describing the topic or issue introduced neutrally: a topic (such as 'school start times') is what the text is about, while the point of view is what the writer claims about it ('school should start later'). The cue is arguability — if nobody could disagree with it, it is a topic, not a point of view. The option about first or third person confuses this with narrative voice, which is a different use of the term.

questions.stem: A student writes this in her editing journal: 'My second and third paragraphs both argued the same point, so I merged them and used the space for a counterargument.' What editing quality is she most directly improving?
options: Control over content, by removing repetition and using the space for a stronger idea
Cohesion at sentence level, by adding connectives between the two paragraphs
Vocabulary, by replacing everyday words with more formal alternatives
Multimodal design, by making the visual layout of the page more balanced
questions.explanation: Cutting a repeated point and replacing it with new material is a decision about what content the text carries — control over content. The cohesion option is tempting because merging paragraphs sounds like a linking job, but she has not added connectives; she has removed duplicated substance. The cue is whether the change alters what is said (content) or only how parts are joined (cohesion).

questions.stem: A draft contains: 'The council closed the pool. The pool was old. Local families were angry. They had used it for years.' Which revision best improves sentence structure without changing the meaning?
options: 'The council closed the pool. It was old. Families were angry. They had used it.'
'The closure of the pool, which was old, occurred, and anger among families resulted.'
'When the council closed the ageing pool, local families who had used it for years were angry.'
'The council closed the pool, and the pool was old, and local families were angry about it.'
questions.explanation: Combining short choppy statements into a complex sentence shows control: subordination signals which idea is the main point and which are supporting details. The version strung together with repeated 'and' is tempting because it does combine the sentences, but coordination alone keeps every idea at equal weight and adds repetition rather than clarity. Look for whether the revision shows the relationship between ideas, not just glues them together.

questions.stem: A student's paragraph reads: 'The author utilises a plethora of literary devices to facilitate the demonstration of the protagonist's isolation.' Reviewing vocabulary choice, which judgement is accurate?
options: The word choices are precise and formal, so the sentence needs no revision beyond a shorter opening
The problem is grammatical: the sentence has no main verb, so it is a fragment that must be rebuilt
The vocabulary is too informal for essay writing and should be replaced with more academic terms
The elevated word choices add length without precision; naming the specific devices would carry more meaning
questions.explanation: Editing vocabulary is about precision, not formality for its own sake; 'a plethora of literary devices' tells the reader nothing that naming the actual devices would not tell them better. Calling the choices precise is tempting because the words are long and academic-sounding, but 'utilises', 'plethora' and 'facilitate the demonstration of' each replace a simpler, clearer word without adding information. Ask what extra meaning a longer word carries — if none, it is padding.

questions.stem: When reviewing a draft, what does improving its 'coherence' mainly involve?
options: Cutting the word count so the piece fits the set length exactly
Making sure ideas connect and follow a logical order the reader can track
Correcting spelling, apostrophes and full stops throughout the draft
Replacing everyday words with longer, more formal-sounding synonyms
questions.explanation: Coherence is about the sense the whole text makes: whether ideas are sequenced logically and linked so a reader can follow the line of thought from paragraph to paragraph. Correcting spelling, apostrophes and full stops is proofreading of surface accuracy, which can be perfect in a text that still jumps around incoherently. The cue: coherence questions are about order and connection between ideas, not about correctness of individual marks on the page.

questions.stem: A student's multimodal report on plastic waste has strong writing but the slides use six different fonts, three background colours, and images with no captions. Which revision best improves control over the multimodal elements?
options: Delete the images and colours so the assessor can focus entirely on the written content
Add more images and animations on every slide so the design looks more professional
Increase the amount of text on each slide so the writing carries the whole argument
Settle on one font and colour scheme, and caption each image so it links to a specific claim
questions.explanation: Editing multimodal elements means making design choices consistent and purposeful, so that visual features support meaning rather than competing with it; captions do this by tying each image to a claim. Deleting all images and colour is tempting because it removes the clutter, but it throws away the multimodal mode the task requires instead of controlling it. The test to apply: does each visual element do a job for the meaning, and are similar elements treated consistently?

questions.stem: When a writer 'proofreads' a draft rather than 'revises' it, what are they mainly doing?
options: Cutting evidence that no longer supports the thesis statement
Rewriting the introduction so it names the audience and purpose
Correcting surface errors such as spelling, punctuation and typing slips
Reordering paragraphs so the argument builds towards the strongest point
questions.explanation: Proofreading is the final, surface-level check: spelling, punctuation, grammar agreement and typographical slips, done once the content is settled. Reordering paragraphs so the argument builds is revision, not proofreading — revision changes content, structure and meaning, while proofreading leaves meaning untouched. The cue is scope: if the change alters what the text says or the order it says it in, it is revising; if it only tidies how it appears on the page, it is proofreading.

questions.stem: A student's draft reads: 'Because of the fact that the council did not consult residents at any point in time, the plan was rejected.' Which edit best improves control over vocabulary and sentence structure while keeping the meaning?
options: 'Due to the council's total failure to consult, the plan was justly rejected.'
'The rejection of the plan followed the non-consultation of residents by council.'
'Because the council did not consult residents, the plan was rejected.'
'The council did not consult residents. The plan was rejected.'
questions.explanation: The original is padded with empty phrases ('the fact that', 'at any point in time'); cutting them keeps the causal conjunction and the complex sentence, so meaning and clarity both survive. Splitting it into two short sentences is tempting because it is shorter, but it deletes the stated cause-and-effect link that 'because' was carrying. Watch for edits that remove wordiness versus edits that remove information — only the first is an improvement.

questions.stem: After finishing an essay, a student writes: 'I read it aloud and heard myself run out of breath twice, so I split those sentences.' Which statement best evaluates this as a reflection on the editing process?
options: It is effective, because it names a checking strategy and the specific change it produced
It is ineffective, because reading aloud only tests spelling and cannot reveal sentence problems
It is effective, because it proves the essay now meets the marking criteria for structure
It is ineffective, because reflection must judge the quality of ideas, not sentence-level choices
questions.explanation: Useful reflection identifies the strategy used, what it revealed and what the writer then changed — this comment does all three at the sentence level. The claim that it 'proves the essay now meets the marking criteria' is tempting because the edit was sensible, but noticing one problem and fixing it is not evidence about the whole essay against criteria. Reflection describes and evaluates the process; it does not certify the final product.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an informative text?
options: To entertain with an invented story
To record events in time order
To explain or describe something clearly
To convince the reader to agree
questions.explanation: An informative text sets out to leave you knowing something, without asking you to take a side. A persuasive text is the tempting confusion — it may contain the same facts, but it is steering you towards a position.
questions.teaching:
Texts are classified by what they set out to do, and the main purposes are worth holding as a set.

One purpose is to make the reader know or understand something, laying out facts, processes or descriptions without asking for agreement — encyclopaedia entries, manuals, science reports. Another is to move the reader towards a position. A third is to entertain through narrative. Purposes do overlap, and a text can inform while quietly persuading, which is why identifying the dominant one matters more than finding a single label.

questions.stem: What is a counter-argument?
options: A question asked of the audience
A point made against your own position
The strongest point supporting your case
A summary of your argument at the end
questions.explanation: Raising the other side's best point and answering it makes an argument stronger, not weaker: it shows the claim has been tested. Ignoring it leaves the reader to think of it themselves, unanswered.
questions.teaching:
A one-sided argument looks strong and reads as weak, because the reader keeps thinking of objections it never addresses.

The stronger structure raises the opposing view deliberately, states it fairly, and then answers it — conceding what is reasonable and showing why the overall case still holds. This does two things: it demonstrates the claim has been tested, and it removes the objection from the reader's mind rather than leaving it there. Setting up a deliberately feeble version of the other side to knock down is the straw-man fallacy, and readers notice.

questions.stem: What does 'evidence' mean in an argument?
options: The tone the writer adopts
The order the points are made in
Facts or examples supporting a claim
The opinion the writer holds
questions.explanation: Evidence is what turns an assertion into an argument — data, quotations, documented examples. Stating a view more forcefully is not evidence, which is the confusion behind a lot of weak persuasive writing.
questions.teaching:
An argument has two parts: what you claim, and what you offer to make the claim believable.

The second part has to be something a reader can check independently — statistics, documented examples, quotations from the text, findings from a study, expert testimony. Restating the claim more forcefully is not it, however confident the wording. Neither is asserting that something is obvious. When analysing persuasive writing, a useful question is what would have to be true for this claim to hold, and whether the writer has shown it.

questions.stem: What is a text's context?
options: The number of paragraphs it contains
The vocabulary the writer chose
The title given to the text
The circumstances in which it was made and read
questions.explanation: Context covers when and where a text was produced, by whom, for whom, and what was going on at the time. It explains choices that look strange otherwise — attitudes, assumptions, and what went without saying.
questions.teaching:
Texts are produced by particular people at particular moments, and that surrounding situation shapes them in ways that are invisible until you look for it.

It covers when and where a text was made, who made it, who they expected to read it, and what was happening at the time — the political situation, the technology available, the attitudes that went without saying. It explains choices that look strange or offensive from a distance, and it is also why the same text read fifty years later can mean something different. Note that the reader has one of these as well as the writer.

questions.stem: What is emotive language?
options: Wording chosen to stir a reader's feelings
Wording that states facts without slant
Wording borrowed from a technical field
Wording repeated for rhythm
questions.explanation: 'Slaughtered' and 'killed' can describe the same event and land completely differently. Spotting the loaded choice is most of what analysing persuasive language involves.
questions.teaching:
Two writers can report the same event with the same facts and produce completely different effects, and word choice is usually where the difference lives.

Some wording is chosen to keep the reader neutral. Other wording is selected specifically to provoke a response — pity, anger, fear, admiration. 'Slaughtered' and 'killed' describe the same outcome; 'crowd' and 'mob' describe the same people. Spotting which choices are doing that work, and naming the feeling they aim at, is most of what analysing persuasive language actually involves.

questions.stem: What does it mean to 'evaluate' a text?
options: Summarise what the text says
List the techniques it uses
Copy out the most important quotation
Judge how well it achieves its purpose
questions.explanation: Evaluating means forming a judgement and supporting it — did this actually work, and for whom? Listing techniques without judging them is the most common way an analysis stops short.
questions.teaching:
Analysis tasks use several verbs and they ask for different things, so reading the verb carefully is the first step.

Summarising asks what the text says. Identifying asks which techniques appear. Explaining asks how those techniques work. And one verb goes further than all of these: it asks you to form a judgement about how effectively the text achieves what it set out to do, for its intended audience, and to justify that judgement. Listing techniques without ever judging them is the commonest way an analysis stops one step short.

questions.stem: What is a multimodal text?
options: One written in more than one language
One published in several editions
One with more than one author
One combining words with images or sound
questions.explanation: Websites, films, picture books and advertisements all combine modes, and the meaning comes from how those modes work together. Analysing only the words misses most of what a multimodal text is doing.
questions.teaching:
Meaning in many texts is not carried by words alone, and the term for those texts reflects that.

A mode is a channel of communication — written language, spoken language, still image, moving image, sound, gesture, layout. A text using more than one is combining channels, and the meaning comes from how they interact rather than from either alone. A film's score can contradict what a character says. A picture book's illustrations can tell a different story from its words. Analysing only the words misses most of what such a text is doing.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of a paragraph?
options: The central point the paragraph makes
The first word of the paragraph
The longest sentence in the paragraph
The quotation the paragraph contains
questions.explanation: The main idea is what the paragraph is arguing or describing overall — usually announced in a topic sentence and supported by the rest. Picking out a striking detail instead is the usual error.
questions.teaching:
Paragraphs are units of thought, and a well-built one develops a single point.

That single point is what the paragraph is arguing or describing overall, and it is usually announced near the start and then supported with evidence, examples and explanation. Finding it means asking what all the sentences have in common rather than which sentence is most striking — picking out a vivid detail instead is the usual error. Reading only these across a long article gives you the shape of the whole argument, which is what makes skimming work.
